## نتيجة البحث (الصق هنا بعد ما يخلص Gemini)

# **Comprehensive Regulatory, Policy, and Architectural Research Report for Wafier: FinTech and Household Energy Budgeting AI**

## **Executive Summary**

The deployment of Wafier—an Arabic Right-to-Left (RTL) financial technology and household energy-budgeting artificial intelligence application—within the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA) necessitates rigorous compliance with multi-sectoral statutory frameworks1. The application ingests synthetic and real-time Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) electricity consumption telemetry (kilowatt-hours), applies deterministic billing transformations in Saudi Riyals (SAR), benchmarks consumption trajectories against household-defined budgetary constraints, and raises graduated financial alerts while providing verifiable advisory outputs through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)4. To achieve regulatory compliance and technical operational readiness, Wafier must align with four distinct Saudi governance pillars alongside international architectural standards1.  
Under the Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) regulatory perimeter, any capability that interfaces with open banking interfaces or processes transaction-adjacent budgetary limits must align with the SAMA Open Banking Framework (focusing on Account Information Services \[AIS\])1 and the SAMA Cybersecurity Framework (CSF), which mandates an audited Level 3 ("Defined") maturity baseline across four governance and technical domains7. Concurrently, consumer financial interfaces must adhere to SAMA’s Key Principles of Consumer Protection, ensuring complete transparency, unambiguous fee and tariff disclosures, and robust dispute-resolution workflows11. If Wafier expands its scope from automated personal budgeting into algorithmic investment allocations or savings-distribution products, authorization or experimental sandbox admission under the Capital Market Authority (CMA) Financial Technology Experimental Permit Instructions is legally required12.  
Under the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA) mandate, Wafier is governed by the Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL), enacted by Royal Decree No. M/19 and amended by Royal Decree No. M/148, alongside its Executive Regulations3. The processing of household energy telemetry—which constitutes identifiable personal data capable of revealing private domestic occupancy and behavioral habits—demands explicit, unbundled user consent under Article 5 or rigorous justification under legitimate interest provisions (Article 6\)3. PDPL Article 26 explicitly prohibits the secondary use of such consumption data for direct marketing, commercial profiling, or advertising without affirmative consent14. Furthermore, Article 29 restricts cross-border personal data transfers, requiring all telemetry processing, model inference, and vector embeddings to reside within sovereign Kingdom boundaries unless stringent adequacy conditions are satisfied14. Algorithmic advisory operations must conform to the SDAIA Generative AI Guidelines (Document SDAIA-P115E) and National AI Ethics Principles, mandating continuous human oversight, algorithmic fairness, and strict mitigation of hallucinations8.  
Billing conversion and advisory calculations must strictly replicate the statutory residential electricity tariffs enacted by the Water and Electricity Regulatory Authority (WERA) and executed by the Saudi Electricity Company (SEC)6. Residential consumption must be deterministically parsed into the official two-tier progressive tariff: 0.18 SAR per kWh for the 1 to 6,000 kWh monthly bracket, and 0.30 SAR per kWh for consumption exceeding 6,000 kWh, compounded by the statutory 15% Value Added Tax (VAT) and standard meter service charges6. Any energy-conservation recommendations generated by the system must reference the technical efficiency standards established by the Saudi Energy Efficiency Center (SEEC) and the Saudi Standards, Metrology and Quality Organization (SASO), particularly standard SASO 2663:2021 for residential cooling infrastructure19.  
The underlying machine learning architecture implements the ITU-T Recommendation Y.3172 standard4. This design decouples the end-to-end data processing workflow across discrete logical nodes: Data Source (SRC), Collector (C), Preprocessor (PP), Model (M), Policy (P), Distributor (D), and Sink (SINK), under the centralized governance of a Machine Learning Function Orchestrator (MLFO)4. Crucially, to prevent non-deterministic large language model (LLM) drift or unverified spend calculations from reaching the end consumer, all budget tracking, threshold checks, and graduated financial alert triggers must execute strictly within a rule-based, deterministic Policy node4. LLM-driven generative components are confined to rendering natural language explanations grounded entirely in verified regulatory and budgetary retrieved contexts4.

### **Detailed Regulatory Content Summaries**

#### **PDPL-ART-05: Consent and Data Processing Mandates**

The Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL), issued under Royal Decree No. (M/19) on 09/02/1443H and amended by Royal Decree No. (M/148) on 05/09/1444H, sets forth foundational mandates regarding lawful basis and consent under Article 53. The statute prohibits processing personal data without the express consent of the data subject, subject to narrow exceptions specified in the law and its implementing regulations3. Consent must be freely given, unambiguous, fully informed, and established via an affirmative action14. In the context of household energy management, interval electricity meter telemetry (kWh readings) constitutes personal data because it enables direct inferences regarding domestic occupancy, appliance utilization, and daily lifestyle patterns3.  
Wafier is legally obligated to implement transparent onboarding consent workflows that separate core utility spend forecasting from optional analytical features3. Bundled or pre-ticked consent mechanisms are legally invalid under SDAIA enforcement guidelines3. Furthermore, Article 5 grants data subjects the statutory right to revoke consent at any time via an easily accessible operational workflow14. Upon revocation, data controllers must immediately terminate telemetry ingestion and execute data purging or irreversible anonymization across all operational databases and cached processing layers3.

#### **PDPL-ART-06: Legal Grounds for Processing and Legitimate Interest**

Article 6 of the Saudi PDPL defines the lawful bases for processing personal data without obtaining direct affirmative consent3. Processing without consent is restricted to instances where: (1) processing achieves a clear benefit to the data subject and obtaining consent is impossible or impracticable; (2) processing is mandatory under statutory law or judicial decrees; (3) processing is necessary to execute a contractual agreement to which the data subject is a party; or (4) processing is essential for the legitimate interests of the data controller, provided that such interests do not conflict with or override the fundamental rights, freedoms, and privacy expectations of the data subject3.  
For Wafier, executing basic contract terms (such as computing monthly electricity bills based on user-provided meter inputs) falls under contractual necessity, whereas utilizing aggregated telemetry for model parameter tuning requires explicit consent or a formal Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA)3. The LIA requires documented evaluation across purpose, necessity, and balancing tests, ensuring that analytical processing does not expose domestic household patterns to unauthorized exposure or secondary exploitation3.

#### **PDPL-ART-26: Commercial Advertising, Direct Marketing, and Secondary Use**

Article 26 of the PDPL governs the exploitation of personal data for promotional, marketing, and commercial purposes3. The law prohibits controllers from transmitting commercial advertisements or promotional messages to data subjects without obtaining prior explicit opt-in consent14. All commercial communications must clearly identify the originating entity and provide an accessible, free-of-charge opt-out mechanism14. Controllers must process opt-out requests immediately upon receipt14.  
Crucially, Article 26 prevents the secondary monetization or profiling of household telemetry for commercial gain3. Granular energy consumption patterns—such as detecting high HVAC cooling loads during peak summer periods—cannot be utilized to market energy-efficiency hardware, contracting services, or financial credit products without explicit marketing authorization3. Energy-budgeting applications must maintain complete operational separation between core non-commercial alerts (such as budget threshold warnings) and third-party commercial marketing3.

#### **PDPL-ART-29: Cross-Border Personal Data Transfers**

Article 29 of the PDPL, along with its dedicated transfer regulations, establishes strict sovereignty constraints on transferring personal data outside the geographic borders of Saudi Arabia3. Cross-border transfers are unlawful unless executed pursuant to an international convention to which the Kingdom is party, necessary to serve vital national interests, required to perform a contract with the data subject, or directed to jurisdictions recognized by SDAIA as maintaining an adequate level of data protection3.  
In the absence of an adequacy decision, controllers may transfer data only under Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) or Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) approved by SDAIA, provided that national security and public policy are not compromised3. For artificial intelligence systems, this requires complete data residency within domestic data centers3. Ingestion pipelines, machine learning training sets, vector database embeddings, and large language model inference endpoints must remain hosted on sovereign infrastructure within Saudi Arabia3. Transmitting raw meter telemetry or user identifiers to foreign public cloud AI APIs constitutes an enforceable statutory violation3.

#### **PDPL-EXEC-REG: Breach Notifications and National Register of Controllers**

The Executive Regulations of the PDPL, supported by the Rules for Registration in the National Register of Controllers issued under Article 34 of the Implementing Regulations, mandate that entities processing personal data at scale or handling sensitive information register on the National Data Governance Platform administered by SDAIA15. The registration profile must detail the legal entity, processing purposes, data categories handled, and the designated Data Protection Officer (DPO) appointed pursuant to Article 32 of the Executive Regulations15.  
Under Article 12 of the rules and the statutory incident response framework, data controllers must notify SDAIA immediately and within a maximum statutory window of 72 hours from becoming aware of any personal data breach involving unauthorized access, disclosure, or corruption15. If the security breach poses a significant risk to the financial security, rights, or personal privacy of data subjects, the controller must also notify the affected individuals without undue delay, detailing the nature of the breach, potential consequences, and remediation measures executed7.

#### **SDAIA-AI-ETH: National AI Ethics Principles**

The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA) published the National AI Ethics Principles to provide an operational governance baseline for ethical, trustworthy, and responsible artificial intelligence deployment across the Kingdom8. The framework is built upon seven core principles: Fairness, Accountability, Reliability and Safety, Transparency and Explainability, Data Privacy, Social Benefit, and Human Oversight8. The Fairness principle dictates that automated systems must not produce discriminatory, biased, or inequitable outcomes across user demographics8.  
Accountability and Human Oversight require organizations to maintain clear human responsibility for algorithmic outputs and ensure that automated decisions can be audited, reviewed, and overridden8. For Wafier, these principles require that predictive spend models and graduated alert thresholds maintain consistent accuracy across diverse housing typologies, demographic segments, and regional climates without systematic bias8. Spend forecasting methodologies must remain fully transparent, enabling consumers to inspect the calculations driving financial alerts8.

#### **SDAIA-GAI-001: Generative AI Public Guidelines (SDAIA-P115E)**

Document SDAIA-P115E (Generative Artificial Intelligence Guidelines for Public, Version 1.0) issued by SDAIA provides specific guidance on mitigating operational and ethical risks associated with Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs)8. The guidelines address key GenAI vulnerabilities, including hallucinations (generating unverified or fabricated claims), prompt injection vulnerabilities, algorithmic bias, and privacy leakage8. SDAIA mandates that entities deploying conversational AI implement technical guardrails, including input sanitization, output filtering, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architectures8.  
Where conversational interfaces deliver financial, regulatory, or technical advisory outputs, statements must be strictly grounded in and cited from verified knowledge base repositories4. The application must clearly disclose to users that they are interacting with an artificial intelligence system8. Furthermore, generative conversational models must never make autonomous, non-deterministic financial decisions or alter contractual budget parameters; all financial calculations must be delegated to deterministic, rule-based computational engines4.

#### **SAMA-OB-001: Open Banking Framework – Account Information Services (AIS)**

The Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) issued the Open Banking Framework in November 2022 under the National Fintech Strategy and the Financial Sector Development Program (FSDP) supporting Saudi Vision 20301. Open Banking establishes the regulatory rules, operational mandates, and technical API specifications that enable consumers in Saudi Arabia to share their financial data securely with authorized Third-Party Providers (TPPs)1. The initial release (Release 1\) focuses on Account Information Services (AIS), which allow fintech applications to aggregate and display bank account balances, transaction histories, and financial standing from commercial banks across the Kingdom1.  
The framework mandates bank-grade API integration governed by the SAMA Open Banking Technical Standards, requiring Mutual Transport Layer Security (mTLS), strict token-based authentication via OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect profiles, and digital signing of API payloads1. Customer consent must be captured explicitly through standardized, unbundled consent journeys detailing the accounts connected, specific data attributes retrieved, access frequency, and authorization duration1. Data access must immediately terminate upon consent revocation1. AIS endpoints provide the verified data feed for tracking utility outflows against household income1.

#### **SAMA-OB-002: Open Banking Framework – Payment Initiation Services (PIS) and Lab**

Under the second phase of the Open Banking Program, SAMA introduced the Payment Initiation Service (PIS) framework and established the SAMA Open Banking Lab1. Payment Initiation Services enable authorized fintech applications to initiate payment orders directly from a customer’s bank account to a designated payee (such as a utility service provider) with explicit user authentication and authorization, bypassing traditional payment card intermediaries9. PIS requires rigorous Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) mechanisms, idempotent transaction handling to prevent duplicate billing executions, and end-to-end cryptographic audit trails for all payment instructions1.  
To support ecosystem security and conformance, SAMA operates the Open Banking Lab, providing a simulated technical testing environment replicating commercial bank API endpoints, security authentication servers, and edge cases1. Participants must connect to the Lab to validate that their systems meet API specifications, latency thresholds, cryptographic signature verification, error-handling protocols, and customer experience guidelines1. Full certification within the SAMA Open Banking Lab conformance suite is a mandatory technical prerequisite before a fintech entity can receive formal commercial licensing or transition out of the SAMA Regulatory Sandbox1.

#### **SAMA-CSF-001: Cybersecurity Framework – Leadership, Governance, and Risk**

The SAMA Cybersecurity Framework (SAMA CSF), first published in May 2017 and maintained as a living regulatory baseline, establishes mandatory cybersecurity requirements for all financial institutions, payment service providers, and fintech entities operating under SAMA supervision7. The CSF is designed to maintain the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of digital assets and customer data across the financial sector25. It is organized around four core operational domains: Cybersecurity Leadership and Governance (Domain 3.1), Cybersecurity Risk Management and Compliance (Domain 3.2), Cybersecurity Operations and Technology (Domain 3.3), and Third-Party Cybersecurity (Domain 3.4)10.  
SAMA CSF evaluates compliance using a structured maturity model spanning Levels 0 through 5: Level 0 (Non-Existent), Level 1 (Initial/Ad-hoc), Level 2 (Repeatable but Informal), Level 3 (Defined), Level 4 (Managed and Measurable), and Level 5 (Optimized/Adaptive)10. Every regulated entity must achieve and sustain at least maturity Level 3 ("Defined") across all sub-domains to be considered compliant7. Level 3 requires that cybersecurity governance structures are formally established, board-level reporting is operational, policies and procedures are approved and consistently enforced, risk management assessments are conducted annually, and complete documentation is maintained for SAMA supervisory reviews7.

#### **SAMA-CSF-002: Cybersecurity Framework – Operations, Cryptography, and Cloud**

Domains 3.3 (Cybersecurity Operations and Technology) and 3.4 (Third-Party Cybersecurity) of the SAMA Cybersecurity Framework establish granular technical controls that must be integrated into software architecture and infrastructure25. Under Domain 3.3, entities must enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) for administrative access, role-based access control (RBAC), secure baseline configurations, centralized log management with continuous monitoring, and automated vulnerability management7. Data protection controls require that all customer information and financial records be encrypted at rest using modern cryptographic standards (e.g., AES-256) and in transit across public networks using TLS 1.37. Penetration testing by accredited independent third parties must be performed at least annually, and critical vulnerabilities remediated according to defined timelines7.  
Domain 3.4 governs vendor risk management, outsourcing, and cloud computing security7. Financial institutions and fintechs must conduct cybersecurity due diligence before onboarding third-party service providers7. Contracts must embed mandatory cybersecurity clauses, data ownership guarantees, right-to-audit provisions, and stringent service level agreements (SLAs)27. Cloud computing hosting arrangements must comply with SAMA's cloud security rules, ensuring data isolation, sovereign hosting within the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and verified incident response integration7. In the event of a significant cyber incident, entities are legally obligated to notify SAMA within 72 hours of identification7.

#### **SAMA-CP-001: Key Principles of Consumer Protection in Financial Institutions**

The Saudi Central Bank enforces the Key Principles of Consumer Protection in Financial Institutions to ensure that consumers interacting with banking and fintech products receive equitable, transparent, and fair treatment11. The principles apply across ten core areas: Equitable Treatment, Transparency and Disclosure, Financial Education and Awareness, Professional Conduct, Protection Against Fraud, Data Privacy, Dispute Resolution, Market Competition, Conflict of Interest Avoidance, and Resource Adequacy11. Under the Transparency and Disclosure principle, fintech platforms providing financial forecasting, budgeting, and transaction aggregation must present all information in plain, accessible Arabic11.  
Computational formulas, estimated financial savings, administrative fees, and any assumptions underlying spend forecasts must be clearly disclosed to the user before decisions are made11. Fintech platforms are prohibited from utilizing deceptive visual interfaces or manipulative friction (dark patterns) designed to mislead consumers regarding their actual financial standing or energy consumption liabilities11. Furthermore, regulated entities must establish an easily accessible, free-of-charge consumer complaint management system11. Complaints must be logged with unique tracking identifiers, acknowledged promptly, and resolved within standard statutory windows, maintaining an auditable digital record for SAMA review7.

#### **CMA-FTEP-001: Financial Technology Experimental Permit Instructions**

The Capital Market Authority (CMA) Board of Commissioners issued the Financial Technology Experimental Permit Instructions on 10/01/2018 pursuant to the Capital Market Law enacted by Royal Decree No. (M/30)12. The instructions establish the regulatory framework for the CMA FinTech Lab—a controlled regulatory sandbox designed to foster innovation in the Saudi capital market12. The FinTech Lab allows local and international entrepreneurs to deploy and test innovative financial technology products, services, and business models involving securities and capital markets within defined parameters, participant limits, and supervisory timelines12.  
The Instructions define the application lifecycle, eligibility criteria, and regulatory exemptions granted to participants12. To qualify for an Experimental Permit (ExPermit), an applicant must demonstrate that the proposed solution is innovative, contributes to the development of the Saudi capital market, is technically mature for live testing with real consumers, and includes comprehensive risk mitigation safeguards13. While basic personal financial management (PFM) and household utility tracking apps do not require CMA permits, any platform that integrates automated investment allocation, securities crowdfunding, debt-instrument offerings, or automated capital market fund distribution must obtain an ExPermit before commencing operations in the Kingdom13.

#### **WERA-TRF-001: Residential Electricity Tariff Restructuring Decision**

The Water and Electricity Regulatory Authority (WERA) governs the electricity tariff schedule across the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, executed by the Saudi Electricity Company (SEC)6. Electricity pricing in the Kingdom is structured around consumer categories: Residential, Commercial, Industrial, Governmental, and Agricultural6. Since the national tariff restructuring of January 2018, residential electricity consumption is calculated based on a two-slab progressive increasing-block tariff6:

> 2. **Tier 2 (Above 6,000 kWh per month)**: Billed at the higher marginal rate of ![][image3] (![][image4]) for all consumption exceeding the 6,000 kWh threshold6.

In addition to volumetric consumption charges, total utility bill calculations incorporate standard monthly meter service fees (determined by meter amperage capacity) and the statutory ![][image5]6. The VAT is levied on the entire sum of consumption charges plus meter service fees6. For software applications forecasting residential electricity bills in SAR from raw meter inputs (![][image6] in kWh), the mathematical transformation in the Policy node must strictly evaluate whether monthly consumption crosses the 6,000 kWh threshold, applying ![][image7] to the first 6,000 units and ![][image8] exclusively to units above 6,000, before applying the 1.15 multiplier4.

#### **WERA-SOL-001: Small-Scale Solar PV Net-Billing Regulations**

WERA has enacted comprehensive regulations governing Small-Scale Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Systems to enable residential and commercial consumers to install grid-connected solar power generation systems (ranging from 1 kW to 2 MW)17. The regulatory model operates on a net-billing mechanism supported by bidirectional smart meters installed by the distribution service provider17. The bidirectional meter independently tracks the volume of active energy imported by the household from the grid and the volume of surplus solar energy exported back into the grid17.  
Imported electricity is billed according to standard residential retail tariff slabs (0.18 SAR/kWh for 1–6,000 kWh; 0.30 SAR/kWh for \>6,000 kWh)17. Surplus exported electricity is credited to the consumer’s account at the approved net-billing feed-in tariff of ![][image11] (![][image12])18. At the end of each monthly billing cycle, the monetary value of exported energy (![][image13]) is deducted from the total monetary charge of imported energy and meter service fees17. If net export credits exceed import charges, the surplus balance rolls forward as a monetary credit to offset future billing cycles18.

#### **SEEC-SASO-2663: Energy Performance Standards for Residential Air Conditioners**

Standard SASO 2663:2021, issued by the Saudi Standards, Metrology and Quality Organization (SASO) in collaboration with SEEC, specifies the mandatory energy performance requirements, rating labels, and test methods for single-package (window) and split-system non-ducted residential air conditioners19. Published in the official gazette Umm Al-Qura and enforced across the Kingdom, SASO 2663:2021 mandates Minimum Energy Performance Standards (MEPS) based on the Cooling Seasonal Performance Factor (CSPF) metric20. Appliances are classified on an energy efficiency star-rating scale, allowing consumers to compare energy performance20.  
The standard establishes that high-efficiency inverter-driven air conditioners conforming to SASO 2663 consume significantly less electrical power (kWh) per cooling unit compared to legacy, low-efficiency units20. When budgeting applications answer user queries regarding appliance upgrades, the RAG knowledge base must draw directly from SASO 2663 parameters4. The system can calculate estimated return-on-investment (ROI) by modeling how replacing an inefficient legacy AC unit with a SASO 2663-compliant unit reduces monthly kWh consumption, directly preventing bracket creep into the 0.30 SAR Tier 2 tariff and delivering tangible SAR savings on monthly electricity bills6.

#### **ITU-T-Y3172: Architectural Framework for Machine Learning in Future Networks**

Recommendation ITU-T Y.3172, developed by Study Group 13 of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-T), specifies the architectural framework for machine learning in future networks, including 5G and complex digital systems4. The standard defines a logical pipeline architecture designed to decouple data ingestion, model processing, policy execution, and action distribution4. The fundamental objective of ITU-T Y.3172 is to provide a standardized, interoperable, and modular structure for deploying machine learning capabilities safely within operational environments4.  
The Y.3172 architectural blueprint is composed of discrete logical nodes: Data Source (SRC), Collector (C), Preprocessor (PP), Model (M), Policy (P), Distributor (D), and Sink (SINK), centrally coordinated by the Machine Learning Function Orchestrator (MLFO)4. The framework establishes strict interface boundaries between probabilistic components (such as ML predictive models) and deterministic policy enforcement mechanisms4. This decoupled architecture ensures that machine learning predictions are rigorously evaluated against operational constraints, regulatory rules, and safety baselines before any output is distributed to end users or downstream actuators4.

#### **ISO-IEC-42001: Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS)**

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the international standard specifying requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS) within organizations34. The standard provides a structured governance framework to manage the specific risks associated with artificial intelligence, including algorithmic transparency, explainability, safety, continuous monitoring, and accountability across the AI system lifecycle34. It aligns AI governance with established ISO standards, such as ISO/IEC 27001 (Information Security) and ISO/IEC 27701 (Privacy Information Management)7.  
For fintech and utility-budgeting AI applications, ISO/IEC 42001 specifies controls across data provenance, model risk assessment, system robustness, and change management34. The standard requires documented procedures for data preprocessing validation, vector database chunk verification for RAG architectures, prompt template versioning, and drift monitoring4. Implementing an ISO/IEC 42001 compliant AIMS ensures that Wafier adheres to international best practices, providing auditable evidence of responsible AI governance that supports domestic regulatory compliance under SDAIA and SAMA frameworks7.

## **Unverified and Ambiguous Regulatory Provisions**

To maintain legal fidelity, the following regulatory aspects have been audited and identified as unverified, historical, or lacking direct public primary authority:

* **Direct Public SEC Third-Party AMI Streaming API Specification**: While the Saudi Electricity Company has completed the nationwide deployment of over 10 million smart meters, there is no publicly accessible, standardized API standard or developer portal (analogous to openbanking.sa) permitting third-party commercial applications to ingest real-time household meter streams directly via customer credentials. Integrations must rely on utility bill scrapers, simulated customer portals, or synthetic demo data16.  
* **Draft SAMA Rules Specifically Titled "Financial AI Rules"**: Speculative references to a dedicated statute named "SAMA Financial AI Regulations" or "SAMA Financial AI Rules" are unverified. SAMA regulates artificial intelligence and algorithmic models within financial entities through the *SAMA Cybersecurity Framework*, *Key Principles of Governance in Financial Institutions*, and individual sandbox admission criteria, alongside SDAIA's national AI ethics principles1.  
* **Mandatory Residential Time-of-Use (ToU) Electricity Tariffs**: Academic and policy studies published by KAPSARC examine dynamic real-time pricing (RTP) and time-of-use tariffs. However, as of 2026, WERA has not enacted mandatory residential ToU rates; residential billing remains strictly governed by the two-slab progressive tariff (0.18 and 0.30 SAR/kWh)6.

### **CHUNK-01**

* **Source Record**: SAMA-OB-001

The Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) released the Open Banking Framework in November 2022 as a cornerstone initiative under the National Fintech Strategy and the Financial Sector Development Program (FSDP) supporting Saudi Vision 20301. Open Banking establishes the regulatory rules, operational mandates, and technical API specifications that enable consumers in Saudi Arabia to securely share their financial and transaction data with authorized Third-Party Providers (TPPs)1. The initial release (Release 1\) focuses on Account Information Services (AIS)9. AIS allows fintech applications to aggregate and display bank account balances, transaction histories, and financial standing from multiple commercial banks across the Kingdom under unified interfaces1.  
For personal financial management (PFM) and household budgeting applications, the framework mandates bank-grade API integration governed by the SAMA Open Banking Technical Standards1. These technical standards require Mutual Transport Layer Security (mTLS), strict token-based authentication via OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect profiles, and digital signing of API payloads1. Under the AIS business rules, customer consent must be captured explicitly through standardized, unbundled consent journeys1. The user must be informed of the exact financial accounts connected, specific data attributes retrieved (e.g., account balance, historical debits), access frequency, and the specific duration of the data-sharing authorization1. Data access must immediately terminate if the user revokes consent1. AIS endpoints provide the verified data feed for tracking utility outflows against household income1.

### **CHUNK-02**

Under the second phase of the Open Banking Program, SAMA introduced the Payment Initiation Service (PIS) framework and established the SAMA Open Banking Lab1. Payment Initiation Services enable authorized fintech applications to initiate payment orders directly from a customer’s bank account to a designated payee (such as a utility service provider) with explicit user authentication and authorization, bypassing traditional payment card intermediaries9. PIS requires rigorous Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) mechanisms, idempotent transaction handling to prevent duplicate billing executions, and end-to-end cryptographic audit trails for all payment instructions1.  
To support ecosystem security and conformance, SAMA operates the Open Banking Lab1. The Lab provides a simulated technical testing environment replicating commercial bank API endpoints, security authentication servers, and edge cases1. Participants must connect to the Lab to validate that their systems meet API specifications, latency thresholds, cryptographic signature verification, error-handling protocols, and customer experience guidelines1. Full certification within the SAMA Open Banking Lab conformance suite is a mandatory technical prerequisite before a fintech entity can receive formal commercial licensing or transition out of the SAMA Regulatory Sandbox1. For budgeting applications, PIS integration enables automated bill settlement when deterministic thresholds are satisfied1.

### **CHUNK-03**

* **Source Record**: SAMA-CSF-001

* **Node Mapping**: ALL

The SAMA Cybersecurity Framework (SAMA CSF), first published in May 2017 and maintained as a living regulatory baseline, establishes mandatory cybersecurity requirements for all financial institutions, payment service providers, and fintech entities operating under SAMA supervision7. The CSF is designed to maintain the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of digital assets and customer data across the financial sector25. It is organized around four core operational domains: Cybersecurity Leadership and Governance (Domain 3.1), Cybersecurity Risk Management and Compliance (Domain 3.2), Cybersecurity Operations and Technology (Domain 3.3), and Third-Party Cybersecurity (Domain 3.4)10.  
SAMA CSF evaluates compliance using a structured maturity model spanning Levels 0 through 5: Level 0 (Non-Existent), Level 1 (Initial/Ad-hoc), Level 2 (Repeatable but Informal), Level 3 (Defined), Level 4 (Managed and Measurable), and Level 5 (Optimized/Adaptive)10. Every regulated entity must achieve and sustain at least maturity Level 3 ("Defined") across all sub-domains to be considered compliant7. Level 3 requires that cybersecurity governance structures are formally established, board-level reporting is operational, policies and procedures are approved and consistently enforced, risk management assessments are conducted annually, and complete documentation is maintained for SAMA supervisory reviews7. Failure to demonstrate Level 3 maturity exposes the entity to formal supervisory actions, regulatory penalties, and revocation of operating sandbox permits7.

### **CHUNK-04**

* **Source Record**: SAMA-CSF-002  
  \[cite: 7, 27\]  
* **Primary Domain**: SAMA Cybersecurity Framework (Operations & Cloud)  
* **Node Mapping**: ALL  
* **Verification Status**: VERIFIED  
  \[cite: 7\]

Domains 3.3 (Cybersecurity Operations and Technology) and 3.4 (Third-Party Cybersecurity) of the SAMA Cybersecurity Framework establish granular technical controls that must be integrated into software architecture and infrastructure25. Under Domain 3.3, entities must enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) for administrative access, role-based access control (RBAC), secure baseline configurations, centralized log management with continuous monitoring, and automated vulnerability management7. Data protection controls require that all customer information and financial records be encrypted at rest using modern cryptographic standards (e.g., AES-256) and in transit across public networks using TLS 1.37. Penetration testing by accredited independent third parties must be performed at least annually, and critical vulnerabilities remediated according to defined timelines7.  
Domain 3.4 governs vendor risk management, outsourcing, and cloud computing security7. Financial institutions and fintechs must conduct cybersecurity due diligence before onboarding third-party service providers7. Contracts must embed mandatory cybersecurity clauses, data ownership guarantees, right-to-audit provisions, and stringent service level agreements (SLAs)27. Cloud computing hosting arrangements must comply with SAMA's cloud security rules, ensuring data isolation, sovereign hosting within the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and verified incident response integration7. In the event of a significant cyber incident, entities are legally obligated to notify SAMA within 72 hours of identification7.

The Saudi Central Bank enforces the Key Principles of Consumer Protection in Financial Institutions to ensure that consumers interacting with banking and fintech products receive equitable, transparent, and fair treatment11. The principles apply across ten core areas: Equitable Treatment, Transparency and Disclosure, Financial Education and Awareness, Professional Conduct, Protection Against Fraud, Data Privacy, Dispute Resolution, Market Competition, Conflict of Interest Avoidance, and Resource Adequacy11. Under the Transparency and Disclosure principle, fintech platforms providing financial forecasting, budgeting, and transaction aggregation must present all information in plain, accessible Arabic11.  
Computational formulas, estimated financial savings, administrative fees, and any assumptions underlying spend forecasts must be clearly disclosed to the user before decisions are made11. Fintech platforms are prohibited from utilizing deceptive visual interfaces or manipulative friction (dark patterns) designed to mislead consumers regarding their actual financial standing or energy consumption liabilities11. Furthermore, regulated entities must establish an easily accessible, free-of-charge consumer complaint management system11. Complaints must be logged with unique tracking identifiers, acknowledged promptly, and resolved within standard statutory windows, maintaining an auditable digital record for SAMA review7.

The instructions establish the regulatory framework for the CMA FinTech Lab—a controlled regulatory sandbox designed to foster innovation in the Saudi capital market12. The FinTech Lab allows local and international entrepreneurs to deploy and test innovative financial technology products, services, and business models involving securities and capital markets within defined parameters, participant limits, and supervisory timelines12.  
The Instructions define the application lifecycle, eligibility criteria, and regulatory exemptions granted to participants12. To qualify for an Experimental Permit (ExPermit), an applicant must demonstrate that the proposed solution is innovative, contributes to the development of the Saudi capital market, is technically mature for live testing with real consumers, and includes comprehensive risk mitigation safeguards13. While basic personal financial management (PFM) and household utility tracking apps do not require CMA permits, any platform that integrates automated investment allocation, securities crowdfunding, debt-instrument offerings, or automated capital market fund distribution must obtain an ExPermit before commencing operations in the Kingdom13.

The Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL), enacted by Royal Decree No. (M/19) dated 09/02/1443H and amended by Royal Decree No. (M/148) dated 05/09/1444H, serves as the primary data privacy statute in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, regulated and enforced by the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA)3. The PDPL applies to any processing of personal data related to individuals residing in the Kingdom, conducted by public or private entities, through electronic or physical means3. The law also possesses extraterritorial jurisdiction, applying to entities outside Saudi Arabia that process personal data originating from individuals located within the Kingdom3.  
Under the PDPL, personal data is broadly defined as any information, regardless of its source or form, that can lead to the direct or indirect identification of an individual, including names, identification numbers, addresses, financial records, behavioral records, and utility consumption metrics3. The law establishes core data protection principles: purpose limitation, data minimization, transparency, storage limitation, accuracy, and robust technical and organizational security3. Data controllers are legally accountable for all processing activities performed by their systems or contracted third-party processors, requiring comprehensive records of processing activities (ROPA) and compliance auditing3.

Article 5 of the Saudi Personal Data Protection Law mandates that data controllers cannot process personal data without obtaining the explicit prior consent of the data subject, except in cases specifically exempted by the Law and its Executive Regulations3. Consent is legally valid only if it is freely given, informed, unambiguous, and granted through an affirmative action14. Bundled, coerced, or pre-ticked consent mechanisms are strictly invalid under SDAIA enforcement guidelines3.  
When designing onboarding interfaces for applications that process household smart meter readings and financial budgets, the consent request must be presented in clear, accessible Arabic, detailing the specific categories of data collected, the operational purposes of processing, the identity of the controller, and any third parties with whom data may be shared3. Furthermore, Article 5 explicitly guarantees the data subject's right to withdraw consent at any time14. The revocation mechanism must be easily accessible and executable within the application interface14. Upon consent withdrawal, the controller must immediately cease processing the data subject’s personal data and execute permanent erasure or irreversible anonymization protocols3.

### **CHUNK-13**

* **Source Record**: PDPL-ART-06  
  \[cite: 3, 14\]  
* **Primary Domain**: SDAIA PDPL Article 6 (Legal Grounds for Processing)  
* **Node Mapping**: PP, M  
  \[cite: 5\]  
* **Verification Status**: VERIFIED  
  \[cite: 3, 14\]

Article 6 of the Saudi PDPL defines the alternative legal grounds under which personal data may be processed without the explicit consent of the data subject3. Processing without consent is lawful only under specific conditions: (1) if the processing achieves a clear interest for the data subject and contacting them is impossible or difficult; (2) if the processing is mandatory pursuant to another Saudi law or judicial ruling; (3) if the processing is necessary to perform a contract to which the data subject is a party; or (4) if the processing is required for the legitimate interests of the data controller, provided that such interests do not override or prejudice the rights and interests of the data subject3.  
Controllers relying on legitimate interest must perform and document a formal Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA)3. The LIA requires a three-part test: establishing the purpose (demonstrating a legitimate commercial or operational objective), necessity (proving the processing is strictly necessary to achieve that objective), and balancing (confirming that the processing does not infringe upon the individual’s reasonable privacy expectations or cause harm)3. In energy budgeting applications, generating core bill forecasts is covered under contractual necessity, whereas utilizing aggregated consumption data for machine learning model optimization requires either explicit consent or documented legitimate interest with anonymization3.

Article 26 of the PDPL governs the use of personal data for direct marketing, advertising, and promotional communications3. It strictly prohibits data controllers from transmitting marketing materials or commercial advertisements to data subjects without obtaining their explicit prior opt-in consent14. All commercial communications must clearly state the name and contact details of the sending entity and must include an accessible, free-of-charge opt-out mechanism14. The controller is obligated to honor opt-out requests immediately upon receipt14.  
Crucially, Article 26 prohibits the secondary exploitation of behavioral profiling data for marketing purposes without distinct consent3. High-frequency household energy telemetry (e.g., detecting peak air conditioning usage or high overall consumption) cannot be repurposed to market commercial products—such as new HVAC hardware, insulation services, or financial credit products—unless the user has explicitly authorized marketing communications3. Budgeting applications must maintain strict separation between core operational alerts (e.g., warning a user that consumption is nearing the 6,000 kWh Tier 2 threshold) and commercial promotional offers3.

Article 29 of the PDPL, along with its dedicated Cross-Border Data Transfer Regulations, regulates the transfer of personal data outside the geographic boundaries of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia3. Cross-border data transfers are strictly prohibited unless the transfer fulfills an obligation under an international agreement to which Saudi Arabia is a party, serves the vital interests of the Kingdom, executes an agreement to which the data subject is a party, or is made to an entity located in a jurisdiction officially recognized by SDAIA as having an adequate level of data protection3.  
In cases where data is transferred to a jurisdiction without an adequacy finding, the controller must implement appropriate safeguards approved by SDAIA—such as Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) or Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs)—and ensure that the transfer does not compromise national security or violate public policy3. For artificial intelligence and cloud architectures, this provision mandates sovereign data residency3. All consumer meter telemetry, financial records, vector embeddings used in RAG systems, and LLM inference endpoints must be hosted on cloud infrastructure physically located within Saudi Arabia3. Ingesting consumer data into foreign public AI model APIs constitutes an enforceable statutory breach3.

* **Source Record**: PDPL-EXEC-REG

* **Primary Domain**: SDAIA Executive Regulations & Breach Management  
* **Node Mapping**: ALL  
* **Verification Status**: VERIFIED  
  \[cite: 15\]

The Executive Regulations of the PDPL and the Rules for Registration in the National Register of Controllers establish mandatory compliance mechanisms for organizations operating within Saudi Arabia15. Controllers whose primary operational activities rely on personal data processing, those processing sensitive data, or those operating across digital platforms must formally register on the National Data Governance Platform administered by SDAIA15. The registration profile must detail the legal entity, representative information, processing purposes, data categories handled, and the contact details of the appointed Data Protection Officer (DPO)15.  
A central obligation under the Executive Regulations is the statutory Personal Data Breach Notification protocol15. In the event of a security incident resulting in unlawful access, destruction, alteration, or leakage of personal data, the data controller is legally required to notify SDAIA within a maximum statutory timeframe of 72 hours from becoming aware of the incident15. If the security breach is likely to result in significant harm or severe risks to the rights, freedoms, or financial standing of data subjects, the controller must also notify the affected individuals directly, explaining the incident, potential consequences, and corrective actions taken7.

### **CHUNK-17**

* **Source Record**: SDAIA-AI-ETH

* **Verification Status**: VERIFIED  
  \[cite: 8\]

The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA) published the National AI Ethics Principles to guide the responsible and trustworthy design, development, and deployment of artificial intelligence across the Kingdom8. The framework establishes seven foundational ethical principles:

> 1. **Fairness**: AI systems must be designed to treat all individuals and groups equitably, actively preventing discriminatory outcomes or systemic algorithmic bias8.  
> 2. **Accountability**: Clear lines of human responsibility and accountability must be maintained throughout the AI system lifecycle8.  
> 3. **Reliability and Safety**: AI systems must operate robustly, predictably, and securely under normal and adversarial conditions8.  
> 4. **Transparency and Explainability**: The decision logic, data sources, and automated outputs of AI systems must be interpretable and understandable to users8.  
> 5. **Data Privacy**: AI systems must respect user privacy, adhering strictly to data minimization and the PDPL8.  
> 6. **Social Benefit**: AI applications must generate positive social, economic, and environmental impact aligned with national priorities8.  
> 7. **Human Oversight**: AI systems must support human agency, allowing human operators to monitor, intervene in, or override automated decisions8.

For energy budgeting AI, these principles mandate that spend forecasts and alert thresholds must be transparent, auditable, and unbiased across different household sizes and demographic segments6.

Document SDAIA-P115E (Generative Artificial Intelligence Guidelines for Public, Version 1.0) issued by SDAIA provides specific guidance on mitigating risks associated with Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs)8. The document highlights the primary vulnerabilities of GenAI models: hallucinations (the generation of factually incorrect, ungrounded, or fabricated information), prompt injection attacks, algorithmic bias, and privacy leakage8. To counteract these risks, SDAIA mandates that organizations deploying GenAI interfaces implement technical safeguards, including input sanitization, output filtering, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architectures8.  
When GenAI interfaces are deployed in consumer advisory applications, all generated factual statements—especially those concerning statutory tariffs, financial liabilities, and energy regulations—must be directly grounded in and cited from verified knowledge bases4. The interface must clearly disclose to the consumer that they are interacting with an artificial intelligence system8. Furthermore, generative conversational models must never make autonomous, non-deterministic financial decisions or modify contractual budget limits; all financial calculations must be delegated to deterministic, rule-based computational engines4.

### **CHUNK-21**

* **Source Record**: ITU-T-Y3172  
  \[cite: 4, 5\]  
* **Primary Domain**: ITU-T Y.3172 Pipeline Architecture (Overview)  
* **Node Mapping**: ALL  
* **Verification Status**: VERIFIED (Benchmark)4

Recommendation ITU-T Y.3172, developed by Study Group 13 of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU-T), specifies the architectural framework for machine learning in future networks, including 5G and complex digital systems4. The standard defines a logical pipeline architecture designed to decouple data ingestion, model processing, policy execution, and action distribution4. The fundamental objective of ITU-T Y.3172 is to provide a standardized, interoperable, and modular structure for deploying machine learning capabilities safely within operational environments4.  
The Y.3172 architectural blueprint is composed of discrete logical nodes: Data Source (SRC), Collector (C), Preprocessor (PP), Model (M), Policy (P), Distributor (D), and Sink (SINK), centrally coordinated by the Machine Learning Function Orchestrator (MLFO)4. The framework establishes strict interface boundaries between probabilistic components (such as ML predictive models) and deterministic policy enforcement mechanisms4. This decoupled architecture ensures that machine learning predictions are rigorously evaluated against operational constraints, regulatory rules, and safety baselines before any output is distributed to end users or downstream actuators4.

### **CHUNK-22**

* **Source Record**: ITU-T-Y3172  
  \[cite: 4, 5\]  
* **Primary Domain**: ITU-T Y.3172 Machine Learning Function Orchestrator (MLFO)  
* **Node Mapping**: ALL  
* **Verification Status**: VERIFIED (Benchmark)4

Under ITU-T Recommendation Y.3172, the Machine Learning Function Orchestrator (MLFO) is the central management entity responsible for orchestrating, managing, and controlling the lifecycle of the entire ML pipeline4. The MLFO manages the instantiation, configuration, monitoring, and updating of pipeline nodes (SRC, C, PP, M, P, D, and SINK) based on predefined deployment topologies and service level agreements (SLAs)4. It interacts with the ML Sandbox—a secure, isolated environment used to train, test, and evaluate machine learning models on synthetic or historical data before operational deployment1.  
The MLFO continuously monitors pipeline performance metrics, such as model accuracy, data drift, processing latency, and node availability4. If model drift occurs (e.g., predictive error rates exceed acceptable thresholds due to abrupt seasonal temperature changes in household energy usage), the MLFO can trigger model retraining within the sandbox or switch to a fall-back baseline model4. Furthermore, the MLFO enforces security and compliance policies across all nodes, ensuring that personal data processing complies with sovereignty and privacy mandates throughout the pipeline lifecycle4.

The upstream segment of the ITU-T Y.3172 ML pipeline consists of the Data Source (SRC), Collector (C), and Preprocessor (PP) nodes, which collectively handle data ingestion, transmission, and transformation4:

> 1. **Source Node (SRC)**: The original entity that generates raw data4. In an energy-budgeting architecture, SRC includes smart electricity meters (AMI), user inputs (monthly budget limits), and external telemetry feeds (weather and temperature APIs)4.  
> 2. **Collector Node (C)**: Responsible for gathering data from one or more SRC nodes securely4. It manages communication protocols, handles connection authentication, buffers high-frequency meter streams, and enforces initial data validation1.  
> 3. **Preprocessor Node (PP)**: Cleans, transforms, normalizes, and aggregates raw data received from the Collector4. The Preprocessor converts raw interval kWh pulses into standardized time-series arrays, removes telemetry anomalies, computes cumulative monthly consumption sums, and applies initial deterministic transformations (such as mapping kWh readings into preliminary WERA tariff brackets) to prepare feature vectors for downstream model ingestion4.

## **Architectural Synthesis and Implementation Roadmap**

Deploying Wafier in alignment with the ITU AI Readiness Hackathon mandates requires seamless integration of Saudi legal statutes into the ITU-T Recommendation Y.3172 pipeline architecture3. The operational mapping establishes deterministic boundaries across every functional node:  
The Data Source (SRC) layer gathers raw interval smart meter readings (kWh), user-defined monthly budget limits in SAR, and real-time regional temperature feeds4. The Collector (C) node securely buffers and authenticates this ingestion stream under SAMA Open Banking AIS security standards and SDAIA PDPL Article 5 explicit consent protocols1. The Preprocessor (PP) node cleanses telemetry, handles missing meter intervals, standardizes time-series arrays, and computes cumulative monthly kWh consumption4.  
The Model (M) node performs probabilistic forecasting using time-series machine learning models (e.g., gradient boosting or LSTM regressors) incorporating regional Cooling Degree Days (CDD with an ![][image29] baseline) to predict end-of-month energy consumption (![][image17] in kWh)4.  
The Policy (P) node receives the predicted consumption and executes non-discretionary, deterministic financial algorithms4. It applies the statutory WERA residential two-slab structure (![][image7] for ![][image18]; ![][image8] for ![][image19]), adds the standard meter capacity charge, and applies the mandatory ![][image20] multiplier6. The Policy node compares the resulting SAR forecast against the user's defined budget and deterministically sets alert flags across graduated thresholds:

* **Level 1 (Normal / Informational)**: Forecasted spend is below ![][image14] of monthly budget.  
* **Level 2 (Moderate Tracking)**: Forecasted spend is between ![][image14] and ![][image21] of budget.  
* **Level 3 (Cautionary Advisory)**: Forecasted spend is between ![][image21] and ![][image22] of budget.  
* **Level 4 (High Variance Warning)**: Forecasted spend is between ![][image22] and ![][image23] of budget.  
* **Level 5 (Budget Breach Alert)**: Forecasted spend exceeds ![][image23] of budget or consumption enters the ![][image30] Tier 2 slab6.

The Distributor (D) node formats evaluated policy alerts into Right-to-Left (RTL) Arabic payloads, enforcing PDPL Article 26 direct marketing filters to ensure that only non-commercial advisory notifications are transmitted4. The Sink (SINK) node renders the final user interface on the consumer's mobile device, displaying interactive spend gauges, consumption forecasts, and advisory explanations4.  
For user queries, the conversational interface utilizes Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) referencing the verified Knowledge Base (KB)4. In accordance with SDAIA Generative AI Guidelines (SDAIA-P115E) and SAMA Consumer Protection Principles, every generated answer regarding tariffs, energy conservation, or appliance ratings must include explicit citations to WERA, SEEC, or SASO standards, eliminating hallucination risks and ensuring transparent consumer protection8. The Machine Learning Function Orchestrator (MLFO) oversees the entire lifecycle, managing model performance monitoring, data drift detection across seasonal shifts, and fail-safe transitions within sovereign Saudi cloud infrastructure3.
